q: How do I prove additionality for an energy efficiency or fuel switch project?
title: Proving additionality for a factory project
short: Show four things with dated documents: you considered carbon credits before you committed money, no law required the change, the project is not financially attractive without credit revenue or faces real barriers, and similar plants nearby have not already made the same change. Small projects may qualify through a simplified route.
audience: Factory owners considering carbon credits for boiler, motor or fuel switch projects

sections.h: Prove you thought of credits before you started
p: Validators check the project start date, usually the date you signed the purchase order or contract. They want evidence dated before it that carbon revenue was part of the decision: board minutes, a loan appraisal note, a consultant's proposal or an email to a project developer. Under CDM rules, projects also had to notify the host country authority and UNFCCC of their intent within 180 days of the start date. A project built first and pitched for credits later rarely passes.

List every rule that touches the change: state pollution board consent conditions, boiler regulations, fuel bans in your city or region, and any energy saving obligation. If your plant is a designated consumer under the PAT scheme, explain how the project relates to your notified target. A change that a consent order already demands is not additional.

sections.h: Pass the investment or barrier test
ul: Investment analysis (CDM Tool 27): build the cash flow from equipment quotes, installation invoices, energy savings worked out from past bills and current fuel prices. Show the return without credits falls below a benchmark and that the result holds if key inputs move about 10% either way.
Fuel switch projects often fail on cost when the new fuel is cheaper per unit of useful heat, so compare cost per useful kcal after boiler efficiency, not price per tonne.
Barrier analysis, used instead of or alongside: show a specific obstacle, such as a lender refusing to fund it or no reliable fuel supply, with letters or quotes, not general statements.

p: Show the technology is not already normal among similar plants in your region. CDM Tool 24 gives a test: count comparable plants using the same measure without carbon credits; if they make up more than 20% of similar plants and number more than three, the measure is treated as common practice. Collect cluster association data, supplier sales lists or a state study as evidence.

CDM Tool 21 sets out simpler additionality for small-scale projects, and some measures sit on positive lists that are treated as additional without an investment test. The methodology you pick, such as AMS-II.D for industrial efficiency, states which route applies. Check the current Verra or Gold Standard rules, since both now restrict which older CDM routes they accept.

example.title: Illustrative cost per useful heat for a coal to biomass switch
lines: Coal: Rs 8,000 per tonne, 4,000 kcal per kg = Rs 2.00 per 1,000 kcal; boiler efficiency 75% gives Rs 2.00 / 0.75 = Rs 2.67 per 1,000 kcal of useful heat
Biomass briquettes: Rs 7,200 per tonne, 3,600 kcal per kg = Rs 2.00 per 1,000 kcal; efficiency 70% gives Rs 2.00 / 0.70 = Rs 2.86
Biomass costs (2.86 minus 2.67) / 2.67 = about 7% more per useful kcal, before the new burner capex
A higher running cost plus capex supports the investment test; if biomass were cheaper per useful kcal, you would need a barrier argument
example.note: Prices, calorific values and efficiencies are illustrative round numbers. Use your own quotes and measured boiler efficiency.

senseible: Senseible keeps your fuel and electricity bills as dated baseline evidence and gives carbon credit eligibility signals from that measured energy data. It does not test additionality, validate projects or issue credits; validation bodies and registries such as Verra and Gold Standard do that.
